title: US Crude Inventories Post Largest Weekly Gain in 3.5 Years as Exports Slump
excerpt: Commercial crude stocks surged by 17.4 million barrels to their highest level since June, defying analyst expectations of a draw and sending oil futures lower.
body:
• U.S. crude oil inventories rose by 17.4 million barrels to 424.4 million barrels in the week ended August 7, the largest weekly build since January 2023.
  • Analysts had expected a 1.4 million-barrel draw, making the actual build a massive surprise that sent both Brent and WTI crude futures lower.
  • A sharp slump in U.S. crude exports was the primary driver, with net imports rising by 1.77 million barrels per day.
  • Gasoline stocks fell by 1 million barrels and distillate stockpiles were nearly flat, offering some support to product markets.

A Surprise Build of Historic Proportions

U.S. commercial crude oil inventories posted their largest weekly increase in more than three years last week, catching markets off guard as a sharp drop in exports left barrels piling up in domestic storage, the Energy Information Administration reported on Wednesday.

Crude stocks rose by 17.4 million barrels to 424.4 million barrels in the week ended August 7, reaching their highest level since early June, according to the EIA. The build dwarfed expectations — a Reuters poll of analysts had forecast a draw of 1.4 million barrels.

Both U.S. WTI and global Brent crude futures extended losses after the data was released, as the massive inventory build added to concerns about oversupply in the market.

Exports Collapse Drives the Surge

The primary culprit behind the inventory spike was a dramatic collapse in crude exports. Net U.S. crude imports surged by 1.77 million barrels per day during the week, indicating that far fewer barrels left the country than in recent weeks.

The export weakness comes at a time when global oil markets are already grappling with shifting supply dynamics. OPEC+ production increases, combined with concerns about slowing demand growth in China and Europe, have kept downward pressure on prices throughout the summer.

Crude stocks at the Cushing, Oklahoma, delivery hub — the pricing point for WTI futures — rose by 1.6 million barrels, adding to the bearish signal.

Refinery Operations and Product Markets

Refinery crude runs rose modestly by 26,000 barrels per day during the week, while utilization rates edged down by 0.3 percentage points to 96.2%. The slight decline in utilization suggests refineries may be nearing seasonal maintenance periods.

On the product side, gasoline stocks fell by 1 million barrels to 208.7 million barrels, slightly less than the 1.2 million-barrel draw analysts had projected. U.S. gasoline futures extended losses on the smaller-than-expected draw.

Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, fell by just 10,000 barrels to 107.1 million barrels — well below the expected 1.3 million-barrel decline. However, U.S. diesel futures reversed losses and rose 0.54% after the data, suggesting traders saw the tight distillate balance as supportive.

Market Implications

The unexpected inventory surge adds to a growing narrative of ample crude supply in the U.S. market. With production holding steady near record levels and export logistics occasionally disrupted, such builds can accumulate rapidly.

For global oil markets, the data reinforces the bearish case that has kept crude prices under pressure since mid-July. Brent crude has already fallen from above $90 per barrel earlier in the summer to the mid-$70s, and a sustained inventory build could push prices lower still.

The week's data will be closely watched by OPEC+ members as they evaluate whether to proceed with planned production increases in the coming months. A persistently oversupplied U.S. market could complicate the cartel's efforts to manage global supply.

What to Watch

Next week's EIA report will be critical in determining whether the export slump was a one-off logistical disruption or the beginning of a more sustained trend. Traders will also monitor Cushing storage levels closely — any continued buildup at the delivery hub could weigh further on WTI pricing spreads.
nri_angle: The inventory surge adds to downward pressure on crude prices, which has mixed implications for Indian consumers and the country's oil import bill.
